title: Cocktail 2 Can See ₹100 Crore from Here. It Might Never Get There.
excerpt: Shahid Kapoor and Kriti Sanon's ₹150-crore romantic sequel is crawling through its third weekend with a 75% drop, mixed word of mouth, and a shrinking screen count. The century is close — but so is the finish line.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Cocktail 2 has grossed ₹92.5 crore in India, falling short of its ₹150 crore budget.
  • The film saw a 75% drop in earnings during its third weekend.
  • Competition and mixed reviews have led to a significant reduction in screen count.
  • Shahid Kapoor's previous release, O Romeo, earned only ₹8.5 crore on opening day.
  • Kriti Sanon is close to her third post-COVID century, needing less than ₹3 crore.

Seventeen days ago, Cocktail 2 looked like it had everything. A killer opening weekend of ₹47.5 crore. The nostalgia of one of Bollywood's most beloved modern romances behind it. Shahid Kapoor at his most charming. Kriti Sanon radiating the kind of big-screen warmth that made the original Cocktail iconic. Rashmika Mandanna adding pan-India electricity to the mix. Director Homi Adajania back in the chair, fourteen years after the film that redefined urban love triangles.

And then the word of mouth arrived. And it was... mixed.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=XXxUqLHq1xg

The Numbers Tell the Story

After a roaring first week that collected approximately ₹70.5 crore net domestically, Cocktail 2 has spent the last ten days bleeding momentum. By the end of its third weekend, the film's India net collection stands at roughly ₹92.5 crore, with a worldwide gross of around ₹140 crore — including ₹30 crore from overseas markets and $1.42 million from North America alone.

Those aren't embarrassing numbers. But they're not what a ₹150-crore production needs.

The third weekend was particularly brutal. Friday brought in just ₹0.75 crore — the first time the film dipped below the one-crore mark. Saturday recovered to ₹1.15 crore, and Sunday nudged it to ₹1.25 crore, bringing the weekend total to a modest ₹3.15 crore. For context, the opening weekend alone was fifteen times that.

Death by a Thousand Screen Cuts

> "It's a "spiritual successor" — same franchise, new cast, new characters."

Part of the problem is real estate. Alpha (Alia Bhatt and Sharvari's spy thriller), Welcome To The Jungle (Akshay Kumar's comedy juggernaut), and the still-persistent Main Vaapas Aaunga have devoured screens across the country. Cocktail 2's show count has collapsed from over 10,000 on opening day to under 1,200 by its third weekend. In the national chains — PVR, INOX, Cinepolis — average occupancy on Sunday sat at a meagre 6.5%.

But screen crunches don't kill films with great word of mouth. Films that audiences genuinely love find a way, even on fewer screens. Cocktail 2's problem isn't competition. It's that the conversation moved on.

The Shadow of a Classic

The original Cocktail (2012) was a lightning strike. Made for ₹35 crore, it grossed over ₹121 crore worldwide and launched Deepika Padukone into a new orbit. That film's secret weapon was Deepika's Veronica — messy, magnetic, heartbreaking — and a soundtrack (*Tumhi Ho Bandhu*, *Daaru Desi*, *Second Hand Jawaani*) that still plays at every NRI house party a decade later. Many diaspora viewers connected deeply with the film's exploration of modern relationships and identity, themes that often resonate with the experiences of Indians living abroad.

The 2026 sequel carries none of those actors. It's a "spiritual successor" — same franchise, new cast, new characters. Shahid and Kriti have genuine chemistry (their *Teri Baaton Mein Aisa Uljha Jiya* proved that), and Rashmika brings her characteristic warmth. But a love triangle needs more than good-looking people. It needs a Veronica — someone who steals the film from under everyone and makes the audience ache.

Reviews suggest this Cocktail 2 is pleasant, watchable, and occasionally witty. What it isn't, apparently, is unforgettable.

The ₹100 Crore Question

With roughly ₹7.5 crore still needed to enter the century club in India, the math is tight. The entire third weekend generated only ₹3.15 crore. Unless weekday holds are miraculously strong or a few screens reopen as competition wanes, Cocktail 2 may fall agonisingly short of the milestone.

It would be Shahid's second disappointment of 2026 — his February release O Romeo netted a dismal ₹8.5 crore on opening day and sank without a trace. Cocktail 2 is a vastly better film than that, but "better than a disaster" isn't the tagline anyone wanted.

For Kriti, the stakes are different. She's already delivered two post-COVID centuries (*Adipurush*, *Tere Ishk Mein*). A third would cement her as one of the most commercially reliable actresses of this era. She's less than ₹3 crore away from that milestone — so close she can probably taste it.

Where Diaspora Viewers Fit In

If you're an NRI who watched the original Cocktail on a projector at a desi party in 2012, the sequel has been available in theatres across North America, the UK, and the Middle East since day one. The $1.42 million North American gross is respectable for a romcom — it's no Dhurandhar, but romantic films rarely travel like action tentpoles. For many in the diaspora, these films offer a vital connection to Indian culture and entertainment, often becoming a shared experience among friends and family living far from home.

The bigger diaspora play will be OTT. Cocktail 2 is a Maddock-Luv Films production, and both banners have strong streaming relationships. Expect a digital premiere within 6-8 weeks of theatrical release — likely on one of the major platforms with Hindi-language catalogues. For those who skipped the theatre run, the couch premiere is coming, offering a convenient way for NRIs to catch up on the latest Bollywood releases, often alongside family back in India.

The Verdict

Kriti Sanon's Milestone
›Needs less than ₹3 crore for her third century.
›Previous hits: Adipurush, Tere Ishk Mein.
›A third century would solidify her commercial reliability.

Cocktail 2 isn't a bad film. It's a decent film that cost too much, opened into a marketplace that punishes anything less than spectacular, and couldn't outrun the ghost of a classic. At ₹92.5 crore and counting, it will likely end as a financial disappointment against its ₹150 crore landing cost — even if it technically scrapes past the century mark.

But there's a lesson here that Bollywood keeps relearning: nostalgia opens a film. Only great filmmaking keeps it alive.
